title: Predictive Coding as a Backprop Alternative (Deepity)
hook: Backprop isn't the only way to assign credit in a neural net. A hobby C++ library reports predictive coding matching it on MNIST — once you make the slow part fast.
key_points: Predictive coding networks replace the backward pass with local error signals that settle through iterative inference.
They appeal to researchers for biological plausibility and continual learning, but naive implementations are painfully slow.
Deepity's author reports 97.73% on MNIST in about 60 seconds of CPU training, closing the gap with backpropagation.
The speedup comes from Direct Kolen-Pollack feedback alignment plus caching to skip redundant forward projections during settling.
Single-author, MNIST-only evidence — treat it as a demonstration of feasibility, not a benchmark result.
content_html: Backpropagation is so standard that it's easy to forget it's one choice among several ways to assign credit in a network. Predictive coding networks are another: instead of a global backward pass, each layer maintains a local prediction error and the network settles iteratively until those errors are small. The idea draws interest for biological plausibility and continual learning, but the settling loop has historically made it far slower than backprop.
extra_html:
What the project claims

Deepity is a local C++ library its author built over a month to test predictive coding in practice. Two changes do the work: Direct Kolen-Pollack feedback alignment, from recent work on accelerated PCNs, and algorithmic caching that avoids recomputing forward projections during the settling phase. With those in place the author reports 97.73% accuracy on MNIST after roughly 60 seconds of CPU training — close enough to backprop, on that task, to call the performance gap closed.

How to read it

This is a single-author project evaluated on one small dataset, so it doesn't tell you predictive coding scales. What it does illustrate is that the usual reason to dismiss these methods — "too slow to bother" — is an implementation property, not a law. The interesting question the write-up leaves open is whether the same tricks hold up on harder problems.

flashcards.prompt: What makes predictive coding networks appealing as an alternative to backpropagation?
flashcards.back_html: Credit assignment uses local error signals rather than a global backward pass, which is more biologically plausible and suits continual learning.

flashcards.prompt: Why are naive predictive coding implementations so slow?

choices.text: Inference has to settle iteratively, repeating forward projections many times
They need far more parameters than an equivalent backprop network
They can only be trained one example at a time

flashcards.explanation_html: The settling phase repeats forward projections; Deepity caches them to skip the redundant work.

flashcards.prompt: How much should you read into the 97.73% MNIST result?

choices.text: It shows the approach is feasible, but MNIST from one author is weak evidence
It establishes predictive coding as superior to backpropagation
It is meaningless because MNIST accuracy cannot be measured reliably

flashcards.explanation_html: A single-author, single-dataset demonstration is a feasibility signal, not a benchmark that generalizes.
